'''Mohammad Sajjad "Saj" Alam''' ([[Bengali language|Bengali]]: মহম্মদ সাজ্জাদ আলম, {{langx|ur|{{nq|محمد سجاد عالم}}}}; 5 January 1947 – 4 May 2022<ref>{{Cite web |title=Prominent Physicist Professor Dr Mohammed Sajjad Alam Departs |url=https://pakistanlink.org/Community/2022/Aug22/05/10.HTM |access-date=2022-10-28 |website=pakistanlink.org}}</ref>) was a [[Bengalis in Pakistan|Pakistani]] and a naturalized [[Pakistani Americans|American]] [[Particle physics|particle physicist]]. His work focused on [[particle physics]] and [[computational physics]]. He played a significant role in several major [[particle physics]] experiments (the Mark II, [[CLEO (particle detector)|CLEO]], [[Gas electron multiplier|GEM]], [[BaBar experiment|BaBar]], [[ATLAS experiment|ATLAS]] collaborations) that led to new discoveries in the area of high-energy particle physics.

==Early life and family==
Alam was born to a muhajir family in [[Dacca]], then part of the [[Bengal Presidency]] of British India (now [[Bangladesh]]),<ref name=IWAS>{{cite web|title=Prof. Muhammad Sajjad Alam|url=http://www.ias-worldwide.org/profiles/prof73.html|publisher=Islamic World Academy of Sciences|accessdate=3 February 2014}}</ref> to a family hailing from [[Kolkata|Calcutta]]. His family moved to [[West Pakistan]] around 1971, after the secession of [[East Pakistan]].<ref name="The News International">[http://www.thenews.com.pk/Todays-News-4-166043-Iconic-war-veteran-MM-Alam-passes-away Iconic war veteran MM Alam passes away], [[The News International]]. Retrieved on 19 March 2013.</ref> Alam was one of eleven siblings: his eldest brother, [[Muhammad Mahmood Alam]] (1935 – 2013), was a Pakistani fighter pilot and war hero who rose to the rank of [[One-star rank|one-star general]] in the [[Pakistan Air Force]];<ref name="The News International"/> another brother of his, [[M. Shahid Alam]], is an economist and a professor at [[Northeastern University, Boston|Northeastern University]],<ref>Institute for Policy Research & Development, [http://iprd.org.uk/?page_id=30 Advisory Board] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190404101927/http://iprd.org.uk/?page_id=30 |date=2019-04-04 }}; [http://iprd.org.uk/?page_id=6291 Dr. M. Shahid Alam] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190404101918/http://iprd.org.uk/?page_id=6291 |date=2019-04-04 }}</ref><ref name=Aksan>Cihan Aksan, ''State of Nature'', [http://www.stateofnature.org/onIslam1.html On Islam: An Interview with M. Shahid Alam]</ref>

Alam decided to become a physicist when his eighth grade science teacher at Saint Gregory High School in [[Dhaka|Dacca]] introduced him to atomic and nuclear physics: "I was hooked; I came home and told my father I know that I would become a physicist," he wrote.<ref name=Born>{{cite web |last=Alam |first=Mohammad Sajjad |title=Born to be a Professor of Physics: The Life of a Muslim Scientist in USA |url=http://roshnionline.com/?p=1425 |publisher=RoshniOnline.com |accessdate=3 February 2014 |date=1 October 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140220011732/http://roshnionline.com/?p=1425 |archive-date=20 February 2014 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

He was the first member of his family to come to the United States, and was one of the first Pakistanis to get a PhD in experimental particle physics.<ref name=Born/> He ultimately became a naturalized American citizen, and lived the rest of his life in the U.S. He was a married man and the father of two children.<ref name=IWAS/>

==Academic history and positions==
Alam began his academic career at [[Dacca University]] (in what is now [[Bangladesh]]), where he earned a [[Bachelor of Science|BSc]] in physics and an [[Master of Science|MSc]] in theoretical nuclear physics. He then went on to earn a PhD in experimental particle physics from [[Indiana University]] in 1975. Alam afterwards spent a year at [[Vanderbilt University]] as a research associate before securing a position at the [[Stanford Linear Accelerator Center]]. In 1979, after spending four years at the [[SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory|SLAC]], he accepted a faculty position at [[Vanderbilt University|Vanderbilt]].{{Citation needed|date=July 2025}}

Alam remained with [[Vanderbilt University|Vanderbilt]] until 1984, at which time he joined the faculty of the [[University at Albany, SUNY]]. At [[University at Albany, SUNY|Albany]], he served as chair of the physics department (2003–2006) and director of the Albany High-Energy Physics Lab. Alam was also the chair professor of physics at the [[King Fahd University of Petroleum & Minerals]].{{Citation needed|date=July 2025}}

==Research==
Alam's research focused on experimental particle physics and computational physics. He was the principal investigator on several major experiments, including the [[ATLAS experiment]] at [[CERN]], the [[BaBar experiment]] at [[SLAC]], and the [[CLEO (particle detector)|CLEO experiment]].

He was the author or co-author of over 1200 refereed papers,<ref name=Born/> 43 of which were his direct publications.<ref name=CV>{{cite web |title=Albany High Energy Physics Lab: Professor Mohammad Sajjad Alam (2010) Curriculum Vitae |url=http://www.ahepl.org/Bio/cv07-8pgs.htm |publisher=University at Albany, SUNY |accessdate=3 February 2014 |archive-date=11 August 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130811044044/http://ahepl.org/Bio/cv07-8pgs.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref>

The major experiments that Alam had directed or played a significant role in include:

*(1972–1974) SLAC E-82 Searches for Exotic Associated with [[Mesons]] Using a Fast Forward Neutron Trigger with the 15" Rapid Cycling [[Bubble Chamber]]
*(1974–75) SLAC E-103 Search for Exotic Mesons Using a Fast Forward Proton Trigger with the SLAC Streamer Chamber
*(1976–79) MARK II at [[SPEAR]] studying collisions. Focus on charm physics
*(1979–2000) [[CLEO (particle detector)|CLEO]] collaboration (CLEO 1.5, CLEO II), studying collisions at the [[Cornell Electron Storage Ring]] (CESR). Focus on charm and beauty physics
*(1992–1993) [[Gas Electron Multiplier]] (GEM) detector proposal for the [[Superconducting Super Collider]]
*(1993–2000) CLEO II Upgrade. Particle Identification System
*(1995–present) Joined the ATLAS detector pixel group at the [[Large Hadron Collider]], [[CERN]]
*(1998–2000) Nominal member of BTeV at FNAL
*(2000–present) Joined the BaBar Collaboration

Alam worked with the [[Beowulf cluster]] class of supercomputers.

He greatly enjoyed mentoring new physicists, supervising more than twenty PhD students.<ref name=CV/> He was also keenly interested in the relationship between science and religion, and taught a course on the subject.<ref name=CV/>

==Honours and awards==
*Dacca University, East Pakistan Overseas Merit Scholarship (1970)
*Excellence in Research Award by the University at Albany, SUNY (1993)
*Abdus Salaam Award for Achievements in Science, Pakistan League of America (2000)
*Fellow, [[Islamic World Academy of Sciences]] (2002)
*Member, [[Pakistan Academy of Sciences]] (2003) 
*[[Institute for Scientific Information|ISI]] [[Institute for Scientific Information#ISI Highly Cited|Highly Cited Researcher]] in Physics
*[[Islamic World Academy of Sciences]] (2006)
